messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 79
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Combat Pilot
- Trauma Type: Police violence
- Pcl5: 80

# Vignette: Elena, Age 79

Elena spent thirty-one years in the air. She flew combat missions in conditions that would make most people's hands shake just to hear about — low visibility, hostile fire, instruments failing at altitude. She learned early that fear was something you acknowledged and then set aside, tucked neatly behind the controls where it couldn't interfere with the work. For decades, that discipline held. It held through a career that broke barriers for women in her country's military, through the death of her husband Rodrigo four years ago, through the ordinary accumulations of grief that come with a long life. What it could not hold against was a Tuesday afternoon in the market district, eighteen months ago, when everything changed.

Elena had stopped to buy tomatoes. She remembers the color of them, how bright they were. She does not remember exactly what triggered the confrontation between a young man nearby and the officers who arrived — only that it escalated faster than anything she had ever seen on the ground. She was pushed hard against a metal stall when officers moved through the crowd. She fell. A baton came down near her head. Someone's boot connected with her ribs. She lay on the pavement looking up at uniforms and sky, unable to move, unable to call out, the breath knocked entirely out of her. A woman who had flown through anti-aircraft fire lay helpless on a concrete market floor, and nobody stopped.

The physical injuries healed within weeks. What did not heal was the way the world rearranged itself afterward.

Elena now lives in a state of vigilance that exhausts her. She wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, her heart going hard, certain she hears boots on the stairs of her apartment building. She lies still and listens until the silence confirms what she cannot quite believe — that she is safe, that no one is coming. By morning she is already tired. She moves through her days carefully, mapping exits wherever she goes, avoiding the market district entirely and, increasingly, any crowded street. She has stopped taking the bus because the press of bodies makes her chest tighten until she cannot think.

What troubles Elena most, she says, is what has happened to her mind. She was a woman who could hold a flight plan, a weather system, and three radio channels simultaneously without losing composure. Now she forgets sentences mid-thought. She sits down to read and finds the same paragraph in front of her twenty minutes later, unread. She describes it as flying through permanent cloud cover — the instruments are there, but she cannot trust them.

The flashbacks come without warning. A man in a dark jacket. The particular sound of a radio crackling. The smell of exhaust and warm pavement. Any of these can return her instantly to the market floor, and for those moments she is not seventy-nine years old in her apartment — she is back down there, ribs cracking, looking up. Her granddaughter visited last month and reached toward her quickly to hug her, and Elena flinched so hard she knocked a glass from the table. She saw the hurt cross the girl's face and could not explain it.

She speaks about Rodrigo often. She says he would have known what to say, that he was always the one who understood how to bring her back to earth when her mind went somewhere difficult. Without him, the nights are very long.

Elena does not describe herself as someone who is suffering. She uses the word *confundida* — confused. She says she has survived harder things. She believes this, and in a certain narrow sense it may even be true. But there is a quality to how she sits in the chair — back straight, hands folded, eyes tracking the door — that tells a different story. The discipline is still there. It is just holding something much heavier than it was built to carry.
